before: A self-join reads the same table in two roles. child is the worker row; parent is the row whose ID equals that worker’s manager_id. Aliases do not copy or change stored rows. Qualifying each column makes the roles clear.

LEFT JOIN keeps every child row. If no parent matches, selected parent columns are NULL. Here Ari has no manager. An ordinary inner JOIN drops that unmatched child. This query follows one management edge; it is not a recursive traversal of every ancestor.
Optional practice: change Dee’s manager_id to 1 in a fresh setup. Predict the one changed report value.
after: A self-join connects a table to itself. Give each use a short name so you can tell its role. One use reads the worker; the other reads the manager.
Match the worker's manager_id to the manager's id. The short names do not copy or change the stored table. They just tell the query which role a column belongs to.

Run this example in a fresh database:
```sql
CREATE TABLE staff(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, manager_id INTEGER);
INSERT INTO staff VALUES
  (1, 'Ari', NULL), (2, 'Bo', 1), (3, 'Cy', 1), (4, 'Dee', 2);
SELECT person.name AS worker, boss.name AS manager
FROM staff AS person
LEFT JOIN staff AS boss ON boss.id = person.manager_id
ORDER BY person.id;
```
The pairs are Ari/NULL, Bo/Ari, Cy/Ari, and Dee/Bo.
LEFT JOIN keeps Ari even though no manager matches. An INNER JOIN would leave Ari out. This query finds only the immediate manager; it does not follow the whole chain of managers.
Create `report(worker, manager)` from the supplied staff table. Keep all four people, including Ari with a NULL manager. Leave staff unchanged.
